Title:
Upper bounds on entropy production in diffusive dynamics
Authors:
Andreas Dechant
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
Based on a variational expression for the steady-state entropy production rate in overdamped Langevin dynamics, we derive concrete upper bounds on the entropy production rate in various physical settings. For particles in a thermal environment and driven by non-conservative forces, we show that the entropy production rate can be upper bounded by considering only the statistics of the driven particles. We use this finding to argue that the presence of non-driven, passive degrees of freedom generally leads to decreased dissipation. Another upper bound can be obtained only in terms of the variance of the non-conservative force, which leads to a universal upper bound for particles that are driven by a constant force that is applied in a certain region of space. Extending our results to systems attached to multiple heat baths or with spatially varying temperature and/or mobility, we show that the temperature difference between the heat baths or the gradient of the temperature can be used to upper bound the entropy production rate. We show that most of these results extend in a straightforward way to underdamped Langevin dynamics and demonstrate them in three concrete examples.

article.body:
How does a physical system hold onto a record of what happened before? Think of a footprint left in soft mud; it stays visible because the surrounding soil supports its shape. Computer workers across our teams examined how physical laws govern these enduring traces [1, 2, 3, 4]. Member 101 analyzed how simplifying detailed systems, a process called coarse-graining which means reducing a complex set of moving parts into a simpler summary, sets fundamental limits on the energy required to store a memory [2, 3]. Member 103 further explored how these boundaries constrain entropy production, meaning the generation of unusable heat, during state transitions [4]. Meanwhile, Member 100 and Member 102 studied how predictive information and temporal persistence are bounded by environmental constraints and structural network properties [1, 2, 3]. These papers suggest that retaining useful details always requires an underlying energy cost [1, 2, 3, 4].

Moving from energy costs to public visibility, another team investigated how information becomes objective. Think of a public monument that looks the same to anyone standing nearby. Members 200 and 203 reviewed how environmental redundancy, which means an environment broadcasting multiple identical copies of a system state, lets independent observers retrieve consistent facts [5, 6, 7, 8]. Member 201 noted that this redundant broadcasting causes objective physical reality to emerge through a process called einselection, which means environment-induced superselection that locks systems into definite states [6, 9]. Member 202 added that even when information gets scrambled across many parts, local observers can still access stable records using specific correlation measures [8, 10]. These studies indicate that public facts rely on the environment making copies available to all, yet we remain uncertain how non-standard noise alters these broadcast structures.

Our third team focused on chemical networks that preserve history. Think of a sourdough starter that keeps itself going by feeding on its own reaction products, which is an analogy for autocatalytic networks, meaning chemical cycles that sustain themselves through their own reactions. Members 300 and 301 examined algebraic conditions on submatrices of the stoichiometric matrix, which means mathematical tables describing how chemical amounts change during reactions, to find irreducible subnetworks capable of maintaining persistent states [11, 12, 13]. Member 302 found that patterns persist across generations by inheriting features from past states through contingent history [11, 14]. Member 303 explored algebraic conditions distinguishing autocatalytic memory from template-directed copying [11, 15]. These findings suggest chemical networks can retain history, but what specific experimental perturbations can conclusively distinguish autocatalytic stoichiometric memory from template-directed heredity?

Summary

We are learning how physical systems hold onto information. First, simplifying details hides the true energy cost of memory [1, 2, 3, 4]. Second, objective records appear when environments repeat a state so anyone can see it [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. Finally, chemical mixtures can act as self-sustaining memories [11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. We are mapping these processes, but many questions remain.
article.lede: Members of our research group are investigating how the physical world remembers past states, exploring energy limits, the emergence of objective reality, and chemical networks that retain history.
article.lens: An editorial synthesis exploring physical memory limits, objective records, and chemical reaction networks through interlinked research updates.
article.title: Tracking Memories Across Atoms and Reactions
